children.text: Useful tools and references for building integrations with DevHub.
Use the official client libraries to integrate DevHub into your application.
Use the DevHub API with any JavaScript or TypeScript application using standard HTTP clients such as fetch or Axios.
Use tools such as curl, Postman, or Insomnia to test API requests and inspect responses during development.
Explore example requests and responses throughout the API documentation.
Experiment with DevHub API endpoints directly from the browser.
Import your API endpoints into Postman to create and test requests.
Use curl for lightweight command-line API testing and automation.
Set up your project and make your first API request.
Explore available endpoints, request formats, and example responses.

The DevHub API provides programmatic access to projects, users, and webhook subscriptions.
All API requests use HTTPS and require authentication unless otherwise noted.
Include your API key as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.
Retrieve projects associated with your account.
Retrieve users associated with your account.
Create a webhook subscription for your application.
Use the API Explorer to experiment with requests and inspect example responses without leaving the documentation.
Webhooks allow your application to react to events without repeatedly polling the API.
Create a publicly accessible HTTPS endpoint that can receive webhook events.
Your application should verify the authenticity of incoming webhook requests before processing them.
Webhook deliveries can occasionally be retried. Design your handler to safely process the same event more than once.
A useful approach is to store the event ID and ignore an event if it has already been processed.
Return a successful HTTP response after the event has been accepted for processing.
For longer-running work, acknowledge the webhook first and process the event asynchronously.
If processing fails, record enough information to diagnose the problem and allow the delivery to be retried when appropriate.
A reliable integration should expect API requests to fail occasionally. Handling errors consistently makes your application easier to maintain and debug.
The request is invalid or contains missing or incorrectly formatted parameters.
The API key is missing, invalid, or expired.
The authenticated account does not have permission to perform the requested operation.
The requested resource does not exist.
The application has exceeded the allowed request rate. Retry the request after waiting.
The server encountered an unexpected problem. Retry the request when appropriate.
Check the HTTP status code first, then inspect the response body for additional information.
For transient failures such as rate limits or server errors, implement retry logic with an appropriate backoff strategy.
Avoid retrying authentication and validation errors without changing the request.

DevHub API requests use Bearer token authentication.
Each project has its own API key. Include the key in the Authorization header of every authenticated request.
Never expose API keys in browser-side JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side applications.
Store credentials in environment variables or another secure server-side configuration mechanism.
If authentication fails, the API returns an appropriate HTTP status code and an error response describing the problem.
See the Projects API reference to learn how to retrieve and manage projects.
Welcome to DevHub. This guide walks you through creating a project and making your first API request.
Before you begin, make sure you have:
• A tool such as curl, Postman, or your preferred HTTP client
Create a project from the DevHub dashboard. Each project has its own configuration and API credentials.
Open your project settings and create an API key. Keep your API key private and never commit it to source control.
Use your API key in the Authorization header when making requests.
A successful request returns a JSON response containing the requested project data.
Continue to the Authentication guide to learn about API keys, request authentication, and credential management.

data.title: New API Explorer

children.text: The DevHub documentation now includes an interactive API Explorer.
The explorer provides example Projects, Users, and Webhooks endpoints and lets developers build a request, provide an API key, and inspect the resulting response.
The explorer also demonstrates loading and authentication error states.
The API Explorer is available from the API Reference section.

data.excerpt: Developers can now experiment with DevHub API endpoints directly from the API documentation.

data.title: Improved webhook guidance

children.text: We have expanded the webhook documentation with practical guidance for building reliable integrations.
These patterns help applications process webhook events safely as integrations grow.
See the Working with Webhooks guide for the complete recommendations.

data.excerpt: New documentation explains webhook verification, retries, idempotency, and reliable event processing.

children.text: DevHub API v1.0 is now available.
